name: Supporters and atmosphere
union: About 72,000 members. Every home match full (about 22,000), mostly standing. About 3,100 travel to away matches. Fans' pyrotechnics cost €242,000 in fines by February 2026, then a club-record €340,000 for one anniversary display; a fan's thrown lighter cost the team a 2024 draw.
dortmund: About 218,000 members (2025). Every home match full (about 81,000), the highest average crowd in world football. About 5,400 travel to away matches. Fans' pyrotechnics cost €139,000 in fines by February 2026; the standing terrace was closed for one match in 2017 after attacks on visiting fans.

name: The ground
union: Opened 1920 in a wooded suburb; over 2,300 fans rebuilt the terraces as volunteers in 2008. 22,012 places, about 18,000 standing. Owned by a club company whose shares fans bought. A €190m expansion to 35,000-40,000 means 18 months at the city's Olympic stadium from 2028.
dortmund: Opened 1974, about 3 km from the city centre; World Cup venue in 1974 and 2006. 81,365 places, including a single standing terrace of about 25,000. Sold in a 2002 cash crisis, bought back in 2006, club-owned since. Named after a local insurer until 2031. No move planned.

name: Ownership and governance
union: A members' association; the professional team was never moved into a company. Members elect a supervisory board, which appoints the president: the same man since 2004, now full-time until 2029. In 2011 it emerged he did 1980s national service in a secret-police guard regiment. Breaking even.
dortmund: A company listed on the stock exchange since 2000. The members' association owns about 5% of the shares but all of the managing company, so members keep control. Members elect the president directly: the former chief executive, elected unopposed in 2025 with 59%. Lost €22m last season.

name: Fans' say in the club
union: Members vote at the annual meeting and elect the supervisory board (the chairman's list of six was re-elected in 2026). The president is appointed by that board, not elected. The fan-and-members department holds a board seat; fan clubs fielded their own candidate for the first time in 2026.
dortmund: Members vote at the annual meeting and elect the president. In 2024 they voted 556-247 to end an arms-maker sponsorship; the vote was not binding and the deal runs to its 2027 end. The outgoing president, who had turned against the deal, withdrew from re-election in 2025.

name: Community work and causes
union: Stadium rules against racism and the far right since 2007, proposed by fans. Turned a planned fan house into winter refugee housing in 2015; a club-linked charity helps refugees find work and homes; a food bank runs at the ground. Lifetime ban for antisemitic abuse (2021). No Pride activity found.
dortmund: A club foundation since 2012 with 100-plus projects. Holocaust-education trips for fans since 2008, a €1m gift to a Holocaust memorial, an anti-discrimination officer. A gay and lesbian fan club is part of the terrace. Integration projects for young refugees. Far-right hooligan groups in the 1980s.

name: Sponsors
union: Shirt: a local savings-platform fintech (since 2025), also on the women's shirts. Sleeve: a heat-pump maker. A betting firm was a top sponsor 2018-2024; current betting ties not confirmed. No arms or state-owned partner found. About 300 partners in all.
dortmund: Shirt: a telecoms group (to 2030), also on the women's shirts. Stadium: a local insurer. Top-tier partners include an arms maker (to 2027, opposed by members) and a betting firm (to 2028, also backing the women's team). Several shareholders are sponsors: a chemicals group, the insurer, the kit maker.

name: The women's team
union: Founded 1969. Professional since 2023; promoted twice in two seasons to the top flight (2025) and finished 9th of 14 there. Plays at the men's ground; record crowd 14,047. Coached by a woman who in 2026 became the league's first female head coach of a men's top-flight team.
dortmund: Founded 2021, starting in the seventh tier; four straight promotions, now third tier and top after six matches. Plays at a 10,000-capacity ground beside the main stadium; record crowd 15,755 (2025 cup tie against the champions). 1,500 season tickets sold for 2026-27. Top flight is the stated goal.

name: Coach and style of play
union: A Swiss coach, 50, hired in summer 2026 after winning his home league with a newly promoted club. Switched from a defensive back five to a high-pressing back four. The fourth permanent coach since a long-serving one left in 2023. One point from four matches.
dortmund: A 55-year-old coach hired in early 2025, formerly in charge of a national team and the country's biggest club. A structured, pragmatic back three; the league's best defence last season. Talks on an extension to 2029 reported. The fourth different coach since December 2020. Four wins from four matches.

name: Squad stability and icons
union: Captain, 39, at the club since 2014 and captain since 2018; his contract was renewed on the club's 60th birthday. Vice-captain in his sixth season. Several regulars left in 2026, including a young striker sold for a club-record fee (about €22m). No player conduct cases found.
dortmund: Captain, 32, out since February with a torn knee ligament; a 26-year-old defender is seen as his successor. High turnover: about €108m spent on mostly young players in 2026, two long-time regulars gone. A midfielder's 2023 anti-trans social posts drew protests from fan groups, including the gay fan club.

name: Academy and homegrown players
union: A modest academy: five graduates in the senior squad, four from the region; one, a Germany Under-21, plays regularly. Most players are bought cheaply or free and sold on; the president says the club must make a transfer profit every window.
dortmund: Known for developing bought-in teenagers and selling them high. Seven academy players in the senior squad, most recruited from abroad at 16 or 17; few play first-team minutes. Past graduates include an American international. A new sporting director brought in to focus on young players.

name: Winning and track record
union: Last 10 seasons: three in the second tier, promoted 2019; peaked at 4th and the Champions League group stage (2023-24), then 15th, 13th and 11th. No major trophy ever; one cup in the communist era (1968). 17th of 18 now.
dortmund: Last 10 seasons: never below 5th, runners-up five times; national cups 2017 and 2021; Champions League finals lost 2013 and 2024. Eight league titles and one European Cup (1997) in all. 1st of 18 now.

name: History and identity
union: Founded 1966 from roots in a 1906 club; under communism the 'civilian' rival of a secret-police team. Near-bankrupt in the 1990s and 2004, when fans gave blood and donated the payments. Fans rebuilt the ground; around 28,000 sing carols there each Christmas. First top-flight season 2019.
dortmund: Founded 1909 by 18 young local players in a coal-and-steel working city. The first German club to win a European trophy (1966); European champions 1997; near-bankrupt in 2005, rescued. Before every match a 25,000-strong terrace sings an anthem shared with an English club.

name: Following from Sacramento
union: About 5,600 miles; no nonstop flights. League matches stream free in the US, mostly Saturday 6:30 am Pacific; no European matches this season. Tickets very hard: about 30,000 apply for each home match. Seven registered fan clubs abroad. Home matches move across the city 2028-29.
dortmund: About 5,500 miles; no nonstop flights. League matches stream free in the US, mostly Saturday 6:30 or 9:30 am Pacific; Champions League around weekday noon on a paid streamer. Tickets very hard: 55,000 season tickets, long waiting list. A New York fan embassy, about 40 US fan clubs.

name: Where the club is heading
union: 17th after four matches under a new coach and style. A €190m expansion of the ground, with about 18 months away from home from 2028. President in office to 2029. Self-funded and breaking even, but needing a transfer profit every window.
dortmund: 1st after four matches; the coach close to an extension to 2029. A new sporting director and a squad rebuilt around teenagers. The arms sponsorship ends in 2027. Revenue fell 12% and the club lost €22m last season; break-even forecast.
